passage:
Monday. Payal came home from her college hostel for the long weekend and, over dinner, launched into a rant: people from the new township were stealing the jobs, ruining the city, all of them. Her older sister Indu felt her own anger rise. She didn't argue. She asked, 'What are you actually scared of, Payal?' Payal said, 'Nothing,' and left the table.
Wednesday. Indu found her on the terrace. Payal was quiet for a while, then said, 'Only three people from my batch got placed. I'm going to end up with nothing.' Indu said, 'That's a real worry. I'd be scared too.'
Saturday. Payal started the same rant again. This time Indu said, calmly, 'I get the fear about jobs. I don't agree that a whole township is the enemy. Can we talk about your placement plan instead?'
Payal rolled her eyes, but she stayed at the table.

qa.q: How many people from Payal's batch got placed?
qa.a: Only three people from her batch got placed.

qa.q: How did Indu feel during Payal's rant at dinner on Monday?
qa.a: Indu felt her own anger rise, but held it back and asked about the fear instead of arguing.

qa.q: Which part of Indu's approach kept the conversation going?
qa.a: Indu took the job fear seriously while calmly disagreeing with blaming a whole township, so Payal didn't feel attacked and stayed to talk.

qa.q: How might Payal have reacted if Indu had argued on Monday?
qa.a: Payal might have felt mocked and dug in harder, and never shared the worry about placements.

grounding: It shows an older sister hearing a scapegoating rant and asking about the fear beneath it, taking the fear seriously while calmly disagreeing with the hatred.

passage:
Saurabh, you've just started teaching. Let me tell you about a student I had, years ago, when everyone still called me Miss Sonali and I was about your age.
He was nineteen, bright, always in the front row. One day in the corridor he started shouting that people like the ones in the new housing colony were ruining everything. Thieves, all of them. The other students went quiet. I felt my own temper rise. I wanted to march him to the principal.
Instead I took him to the empty staff room and asked, 'What are you really afraid of?'
He was silent a long time. Then: 'My father's shop is losing money. I think I'll have to drop out.'
I said, 'That's a real fear. I'm sorry.' And then, calmly, 'But blaming a whole colony won't save the shop. Can we talk about what might?'
He came back the next week. And the week after.
That's all I did, Saurabh. I listened for the fear first.

qa.q: What did the student say his father's shop was doing?
qa.a: He said his father's shop was losing money.

qa.q: How did Sonali feel when the student started shouting in the corridor?
qa.a: She felt angry, her own temper rising, and wanted to march him to the principal.

qa.q: What does Sonali want Saurabh to take from this story as a new teacher?
qa.a: That listening for the fear beneath a hateful rant, while calmly disagreeing with the blame, keeps a student talking.

qa.q: What might the student have felt when Sonali said 'That's a real fear. I'm sorry'?
qa.a: He may have felt heard for the first time, which made him willing to come back and talk again.

grounding: It shows a teacher hearing a student's scapegoating rant, asking what he is afraid of, and calmly disagreeing while taking the fear seriously.
